claims.text: Compelling new hires to make active decisions about 401(k) enrollment raises the initial fraction that enroll by 28 percentage points relative to a standard opt-in enrollment procedure.
Active decision enrollment produces a savings distribution three months after hire that would take 30 months to achieve under standard opt-in enrollment.
Active decisions are optimal when consumers have a strong propensity to procrastinate and savings preferences are highly heterogeneous.
Financial illiteracy favors default enrollment over active decision enrollment.

evidence.description: Compelling new hires to make active decisions about 401(k) enrollment raises the initial fraction that enroll by 28 percentage points relative to a standard opt-in enrollment procedure.
Active decision enrollment produced a savings distribution three months after hire that would take 30 months to achieve under standard enrollment.
Derived from a theoretical model of 401(k) enrollment under conditions of high procrastination and preference heterogeneity.
Derived from the theoretical model showing conditions under which default enrollment is favored over active decision enrollment due to financial illiteracy.

methodologies.name: Empirical analysis and theoretical modeling of 401(k) enrollment regimes
methodologies.description: The authors analyze empirical 401(k) enrollment among new hires under an active decision regime versus standard opt-in enrollment and develop an analytical model to derive conditions for optimal enrollment regimes.
